newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK activists fly to Taiwan to join flotilla protest.
newsitem.headline: HK activists fly to Taiwan to join flotilla protest.

text.p: Hong Kong activists, ignoring a warning from Taiwan, set off on Saturday for a cluster of disputed islands in the East China Sea to challenge Japan's claim of sovereignty.
The 80 activists flew to Taiwan to join demonstrators preparing to sail on Monday morning to the islands, which are claimed by Beijing, Taipei and Tokyo.
Taiwan hinted on Friday it might halt the protest voyage, saying the private flotilla could be illegal. It has also said it would not provide marine protection.

Anti-Japanese sentiment in China, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau has flared in recent months after Japanese extremists erected a lighthouse and flags on the islands, which Japan calls the Senkakus and which China claims as the Diaoyu isles.
Protester leader Tsang Kin-shing said this showed the Taiwan government was incompetent to stand up against Japan.
"We will sail to the islands as planned," he told reporters. "In fact, we are not surprised about this coming from an incompetent government, like the Taiwan government."

Democratic Party legislator Albert Chan was outraged. "As a government for Chinese people, not only does it (the Taiwan government) not help Chinese to return to their soil, but instead it intimidates Chinese people from going there," he told reporters.

The activists staged a rally at a park near the airport before boarding their flight to Taiwan. They shouted "Down with Japanese militarism" and "Protect Diaoyu Islands with our life". At the airport, about 100 supporters saw them off.
Tsang called on the Chinese and Taiwan government to take action on the islands row.

"Now Chinese around the world have united," he said. "I hope the two (Chinese) governments can wake up to the fact that Japan will not simply give up its claim. They will have to get tough with Japan in order to get the isles back."

Members of the Preparatory Committee, the influential China-appointed body overseeing the handover of Hong Kong sovereignty from Britain to China next year, petitioned Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen in Beijing to put pressure on Japan over the isles row.
Hong Kong will revert to China's control on July 1, next year, ending more than 150 years of British colonial rule.

Governor Chris Patten on Friday urged the activists to be careful. "I do hope they will do everything possible not to put themselves or others in any physical danger, however strongly they feel about the issue in question," he said.

Patten also offered condolences to the family of activist David Chan who drowned near the disputed isles last week after jumping off a ship to protest against Japan's sovereignty claim. His two-day funeral began on Saturday.
Japan has claimed the potentially resource-rich islands since 1895 and refuses to admit that their sovereignty is open to discussion. China has claimed them for centuries.
